newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy plays down security threat from League.
newsitem.headline: Italy plays down security threat from League.

text.p: The government on Monday ruled out special security at planned "independence day" rallies by the separatist Northern League next weekend as its leader Umberto Bossi fired another verbal broadside at a united Italy.

Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano, who has overall charge of police, said no extraordinary measures would be taken for the event, which will coincide with a rash of counter-demonstrations against Bossi's secessionist drive.
"We will adopt the measures which we always take to guarantee the free and peaceful conduct of important political rallies, whatever their origin and whatever their inspiration," Napolitano said.
He told reporters in Milan, where the League has its national headquarters, that next weekend's events had been "over-dramatised". "We trust everyone will display a sense of responsibility," he said.

Bossi plans to proclaim an independent "republic" in northern Italy next Sunday at a rally in Venice, the climax to three days of rallies and demonstrations along the River Po which he hopes will attract at least one million supporters.

He said his party would establish a "provisional government" of Padania, the name he has given his purported republic, to handle defence, monetary affairs and foreign relations pending what he said would be full independence within a year.
"Today he's on a visit to what used to be Roman possessions. Soon they will be the cities and metropolises of a great people, an unbeatable people called the people of Padania," Bossi said.
Italy's centre-left government has resisted calls from some political quarters to ban Bossi's "independence day" rallies, reasoning that a crackdown would play into his hands.
It has appealed to organisers of counter-rallies in support of a united Italy, many of which will also take place on the Po, to demonstrate peaceably.

The League built its support in affluent northern Italy on discontent with corruption, central government inefficiency and high taxes but Bossi's separatist drive does not appear to have found substantial favour in the north.
The movement won 3.7 million votes at a general election in April.

Although the result made the League Italy's fourth biggest party, Bossi's critics saw that his failure to secure the balance of power in parliament explains his recent switch from a federalist to a secessionist platform.
"Bossi has accelerated his actions simply because politically he counts for nothing," Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Sunday night.

The parties which support Prodi's government, as well as centre-right opposition parties, are united against the secessionist drive. They say the answer to justified frustration among northerners lies in federal reform.
